evidence.claim: By 1964, the Navy supported a bridge with at least 200 feet of ship clearance. The curved alignment provided the extra length needed to reach that height without an excessive grade.
evidence.quote: By 1964 the Navy supported a bridge if there was at least 200 feet (61 m) of clearance for ships which operate out of the nearby Naval Base San Diego to pass underneath it. To achieve this clearance with a reasonable grade, the bridge length was increased by taking a curved path rather than a more direct path to Coronado.

evidence.claim: The bridge opened in 1969, providing a direct connection across the bay.

evidence.claim: Orange Avenue once carried streetcars as well as street traffic; they ran here in the 1910s and were retired in 1939.
evidence.quote: In the 1910s, Coronado had streetcars running on Orange Avenue. These streetcars became a fixture of the city until their retirement in 1939.

evidence.claim: The Hotel del Coronado anchors the town's resort history: the wooden Victorian beachfront hotel opened in 1888.
evidence.quote: When the hotel opened in 1888, it was the largest resort hotel in the world.

evidence.claim: the wooden Victorian beachfront hotel
evidence.quote: A rare surviving example of an American architectural genre—the wooden Victorian beach resort

evidence.claim: Its construction depended largely on Chinese immigrant labor from San Francisco and Oakland.
evidence.quote: Labor was provided largely by Chinese immigrants from San Francisco and Oakland.

evidence.claim: Raw lumber arrived from Humboldt Bay, then was finished in planing mills built on site.
evidence.quote: Planing mills were built on site to finish raw lumber shipped directly from the Dolbeer & Carson lumber yards on the shores of Humboldt Bay.

evidence.claim: The historic front facade and veranda were restored in 2021, part of a continuing sequence of renovations.
evidence.quote: In 2021, the hotel's historic main lobby, front facade, and front veranda were restored

evidence.claim: The hotel received National Historic Landmark designation in 1977, recognizing a surviving wooden Victorian beach resort.
evidence.quote: A rare surviving example of an American architectural genre—the wooden Victorian beach resort—it was designated a California Historical Landmark in 1970 and a National Historic Landmark in 1977.

evidence.claim: The Silver Strand is a low, narrow, seven-mile sandy isthmus connecting Coronado and Imperial Beach.
evidence.quote: Silver Strand, or simply The Strand, is a low, narrow, sandy isthmus or a human-constructed tombolo 7 miles (11 km) long in San Diego County, California, partially within Silver Strand State Beach. It connects Coronado with Imperial Beach.

evidence.claim: Together with Point Loma, it shelters and defines San Diego Bay.
evidence.quote: Together with the Point Loma peninsula it shelters and defines San Diego Bay.

evidence.claim: Silver shells along 2.5 miles of its ocean shore gave the strand its name.
evidence.quote: The ocean side of the strand features 2.5 miles (4.0 km) of coastline trimmed with silver shells (thus named Silver Strand).

evidence.claim: Silver Strand State Beach includes both bay and ocean beaches.
evidence.quote: Silver Strand State Beach, a popular beach for camping, bird watching, and bicycling, is located in the middle of the isthmus and includes both bay and ocean beaches.

evidence.claim: The beaches north and south of the state beach belong to the Department of Defense: Naval Amphibious Base Coronado lies to the north and Silver Strand Training Complex to the south.
evidence.quote: The beaches north and south of the state beach are Department of Defense property. North of it is Naval Amphibious Base Coronado and south of it is Silver Strand Training Complex.
